author: EmuCore - Hub
title: GScube: PlayStation 2 technology in a real-time cinema experiment
summary: Sony demonstrated sixteen modified PS2-derived processing units at SIGGRAPH 2000. The system had to distribute graphics work and combine the resulting images.
heroAlt: Original architectural illustration of sixteen processing tiles feeding a single display compositor

blocks.text: Console technology in a larger system

Sony demonstrated GScube at SIGGRAPH in 2000. It used sixteen modified processing units based on Emotion Engine and Graphics Synthesizer technology. Demonstrations from that year connected the system to an external SGI computer. This was an experiment in professional graphics, with custom hardware and memory arrangements, rather than a PS2 accessory for consumers.

Distributing rendering across processors creates another problem: combining their output into a correct final image. Graphics research from that period discussed GScube alongside tiled and depth-based composition systems. Each approach needs coordinated output. The diagram illustrates this many-to-one relationship; it is a conceptual explanation rather than a photograph or wiring plan of GScube.
Demonstrations connected games and film work

Reports from that period describes real-time film-related demonstrations, including an Antz scene prepared with Criterion and PDI. They explored interactive control of complex imagery. The external computer and modified rendering units were part of the setup. The demonstration therefore cannot establish that a single consumer PS2 could reproduce the same scene at the same quality.
Throughput depends on more than arithmetic

Maximum rendering rates and arithmetic throughput describe particular operations. They do not account for every cost of preparing a scene, transferring data and combining images. Increasing the number of processors still leaves those tasks to solve. GScube provides a useful example of why the complete rendering system matters when interpreting impressive performance figures.
A distinct part of PlayStation history

GScube shows Sony investigating a professional use for technology related to its consumer console. It belongs to PS2 history because of that shared architecture, but its purpose and resources were different. Keeping the distinction clear helps explain both the fixed limits of a consumer console and the possibilities explored by a much larger graphics installation.
